title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 9
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a memoir-style narrative, a social science passage on medical history, paired humanities passages on library design and a natural science passage on seagrass), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, 4 passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Humanities — paired passages A and B (library design)

items: Sit somewhere quiet with no phone and no dictionary. Keep scrap paper and a pencil for your passage map.
Start the timer and do not pause it. The section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about **10 minutes per passage**: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
For the paired passages, read Passage A and answer its questions, then Passage B and its questions, and do the questions about both passages last.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so **answer every question**. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score.

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original memoir-style story. The narrator remembers the first years after her family moved from Cairo to Montreal, Canada. The family is fictional.

[1] We arrived in Montreal in January, which my father later admitted was a poor piece of planning. In Cairo he had been a surgeon with twenty years of operations behind him and a brass nameplate beside his clinic door. In Montreal he was a man in a borrowed coat who could not yet work as a doctor, because his qualifications had to be examined, his exams retaken, and his French—learned at school and not used since—made fluent enough to talk to patients.

[2] I was thirteen and spoke no French at all. The school put me in what it called a welcome class, a room of twenty children from eleven countries whose only shared language, for the first months, was pointing. Our teacher, Madame Roy, spoke slowly and drew constantly. By March I could ask for a pencil, refuse a second helping and argue, badly, about football. By May I was dreaming in a mixture of Arabic and French that I could not have explained to anyone in either language.

[3] Children learn languages the way water finds cracks. My father learned French the way he had once learned anatomy: from the beginning, in order, with a dictionary. Every evening he sat at our kitchen table with a grammar book, a notebook ruled into neat columns and a cup of tea he always forgot to drink. He copied verb tables. He recited them under his breath while he washed the dishes. He would not move on to a new tense until he had mastered the last one, and so, while I raced ahead, careless and loud, he advanced like a man crossing a river on stones he had tested one by one.

[4] It was not long before I became the family's translator. I spoke to the landlord about the radiator that knocked all night. I explained to the woman at the bank why my father's name appeared in three different spellings on three different documents. At the pharmacy I asked for cough syrup while he stood beside me, nodding as though he were checking my work. I enjoyed it, I admit. For the first time in my life, adults needed me, and I wore the importance of it the way one wears a new coat.

[5] What I did not notice was what it cost him. One Saturday at the market, a stallholder asked my father a question about the apples, and before he could answer, I answered for him. The stallholder laughed and said something quick that I understood and my father did not—something about how the children always end up running things. My father smiled politely. On the walk home he carried both bags and said nothing, and I talked enough for both of us.

[6] That night I came into the kitchen for water and found him at the table as usual, but he was not copying verbs. He was reading aloud from a children's book I had brought home from school months earlier and forgotten, a story about a bear who loses his hat. He read each sentence twice, slowly, his finger under the words. When he noticed me in the doorway, he closed the book, not quickly, but carefully, as he did everything.

[7] "It is a good book," he said in French. "The bear is very patient." His accent was heavy, and his grammar was perfect.

[8] I wanted to say something kind, but all I could find was the truth: I had never once asked him how his studying was going. So I sat down across from him and asked, in French, what he had learned that day. He told me. It took him a long time, and he had to stop twice to search for a word, and I did not supply either one.

[9] After that we had a rule, though neither of us ever said it out loud. At the pharmacy and the bank, I stood half a step behind him. When he hesitated, I waited. Sometimes the person across the counter waited too, and sometimes they did not, and when they did not, my father simply began the sentence again.

[10] He passed his examinations three years later, on his second attempt. By then my French was faster than his and always would be, but I had stopped thinking of speed as the measure of anything. I still have the notebook with the ruled columns. On its last page, in his careful hand, is the bear's story, copied out in full.
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
c: A narrator explains why children learn new languages more easily than adults do.
An adult narrator recalls how, after moving to a new country, she came to respect her father's slow and determined way of learning a language.
A father describes the examinations he had to pass before he could work as a doctor in Canada.
A girl describes her difficult first year in a welcome class and the friends she made there.
questions.e: The passage follows the narrator from enjoying her role as translator to standing "half a step behind" her father, and paragraph 10 sums up her new view. The idea that children learn faster is only one detail, not the subject of the whole passage.
ce: Too narrow: only one sentence ("the way water finds cracks") compares children and adults; the passage is about the narrator and her father.
Right: the story moves from the narrator speaking for her father to waiting for him, and paragraph 10 states her changed view.
Wrong narrator and wrong focus: the daughter tells the story, and the exams are mentioned only briefly.
Too narrow: the welcome class appears only in paragraph 2, and no friendships are described.

questions.q: According to the passage, the narrator's father could not yet work as a doctor in Montreal because:
c: his qualifications had to be examined and his French improved.
he had decided to retire from surgery after twenty years.
he had left his documents behind in Cairo.
the hospitals in the city had no jobs for surgeons.

Not stated: he was trying to return to medicine, not retire.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 mentions his documents at the bank.
Not in the passage: no hospital or job shortage is mentioned.

c: her teacher had asked her to practise French outside school.
her father paid her for helping him.

questions.q: It can reasonably be inferred from paragraph 5 that the father's silence on the walk home suggests that he:
c: was angry with the stallholder for charging too much for the apples.
disapproved of the apples his daughter had chosen.
was hurt at being made to seem dependent on his daughter.
was too tired to talk after carrying the bags.

ce: Not supported: no price problem is mentioned.

Right: the stallholder joked that children "end up running things," and the narrator says she did not notice "what it cost him."
Too literal: the narrator links his silence to what the episode "cost him," not to tiredness.

show that the father had given up studying grammar.
describe the narrator's favourite book from her welcome class.
present a private moment that shows the father's continued effort and leads the narrator to change her behaviour.

questions.p:
Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the history of medicine.

[1] In the 1840s, a woman about to give birth in Vienna's General Hospital had good reason to care which day she arrived. The hospital's maternity department was divided into two clinics, which admitted patients on alternate days. The First Clinic trained medical students and was run by doctors; the Second Clinic trained midwives. In the First Clinic, far more mothers died of childbed fever, an infection that could kill within days of delivery. The difference was well known in the city, and some women, it was reported, preferred to give birth in the street rather than be taken to the doctors' clinic.

[2] Ignaz Semmelweis, a young Hungarian doctor who became an assistant in the First Clinic in 1846, was troubled by the gap. He worked through the possible explanations one by one. Crowding could not be the cause, because the Second Clinic was, if anything, more crowded. Weather and "bad air" affected both clinics equally. Even the priest who walked through the First Clinic ringing a bell on his way to the dying was asked to change his route, in case fear itself was making women ill. Nothing changed.

[3] The answer came through a death. In 1847 a colleague, Jakob Kolletschka, was accidentally cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy and died of an illness whose signs closely resembled those of childbed fever. Semmelweis drew a bold conclusion. Doctors and students in the First Clinic often came to the delivery rooms directly from examining bodies in the autopsy room; midwives did not perform autopsies. Something from the dead, he reasoned—he called it "cadaverous particles"—was being carried on the hands of the doctors themselves.

[4] In May 1847 he ordered everyone entering the First Clinic to wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime, chosen because it removed the smell of the autopsy room better than ordinary soap. Within months, the death rate fell sharply, to a level close to that of the midwives' clinic. By any modern standard, it was one of the most convincing results in the history of medicine.

[5] Yet the idea spread slowly, and Semmelweis himself was soon pushed aside. Historians have offered several explanations, and none of them is simply that his colleagues were foolish. First, his theory did not fit the medical thinking of the time. Many doctors believed that diseases arose from imbalances within the body or from poisoned air, and the idea that invisible matter on a gentleman's clean-looking hands could kill was hard to accept—and, for some, insulting. Second, Semmelweis was slow to publish. For more than a decade he left it largely to others to describe his findings, and his own book did not appear until 1861. Third, when he did answer his critics, he did so angrily, accusing some of them in open letters of being responsible for women's deaths.

[6] Some historians add a fourth point: Semmelweis had the right practice but an incomplete explanation. He could show that washing worked, but he could not show what, exactly, the "particles" were. That explanation arrived only in the following decades, as Louis Pasteur's work on microorganisms helped to build the germ theory of disease and the surgeon Joseph Lister began using carbolic acid to keep wounds clean. Semmelweis did not live to see this change. He died in 1865, at the age of forty-seven.

[7] Today Semmelweis is often presented as a lonely hero defeated by stubborn rivals, and there is truth in that picture. But the more useful lesson may be less dramatic. Good evidence does not travel on its own. It needs an explanation that fits, or can change, what people already believe; it needs to be published where others can test it; and it needs to be communicated in a way that invites agreement rather than resistance. Semmelweis had the evidence. What he lacked were the other three.

[8] The point is not only historical. Modern hospitals still struggle to persuade busy staff to clean their hands as often as the evidence says they should, and campaigns that simply repeat the data tend to work less well than those that change daily routines, place cleaning stations where they are needed and use respected colleagues as examples. More than a century and a half after Semmelweis, the problem he faced has not disappeared. It has only changed its clothes.

arguing that Semmelweis's colleagues rejected him because they were foolish.

explaining why a convincing medical discovery was slow to be accepted and what this suggests about how evidence spreads.

Passage III — Humanities (Paired Passages)

HUMANITIES: Passage A is from an original essay by an architect who designs public libraries. Passage B is from an original essay by a librarian. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "The Library as a Living Room"

[1] For most of their history, libraries were designed around a problem of storage. Books were rare and costly, and the buildings that held them were built like treasuries: thick walls, high windows, long reading tables under the watchful eye of the librarian's desk. The reader was a guest in a house that belonged, in a sense, to the books.

[2] That problem has largely been solved. A single tablet can hold more text than many town libraries once did, and much of what people come to look up can be found from home. If libraries are still to matter, their buildings must be designed around a different problem—not where to keep information, but where people can gather to use it, discuss it and make things with it.

[3] In the libraries my studio designs, shelves no longer fill the centre of the floor. They line the walls or are grouped into smaller rooms, freeing the main hall for tables that can be pushed together, rooms that can be booked for a homework club or a language class, a workshop with sewing machines and a 3D printer, and, yes, a café. Large windows open the interior to the street, so that someone walking past can see what is happening inside and feel invited to join in.

[4] Critics complain that such buildings are noisy and look more like airports than places of study. The noise is real, but it is a sign of success. In many neighbourhoods the library is the last indoor public space where a person may stay all afternoon without buying anything. Teenagers with nowhere else to meet, older people who live alone and parents with small children all need such a space, and they need it to be lively and welcoming, not hushed and forbidding.

[5] Silence still has a place; we simply give it its own rooms. What we refuse to do is let a minority who want perfect quiet decide the shape of a building that should belong to everyone.

PASSAGE B — "In Defence of the Quiet Room"

[1] I have worked in public libraries for twenty-six years, and I have welcomed most of the changes I have seen. Our computers are always busy. Our children's corner is loud, and it should be. I would not want to return to the days when a librarian's main job was to say "Shh."

[2] But I have watched with growing concern as new library buildings treat quiet as an afterthought. In one bright new branch I visited, the "silent study room" was a glass box beside the café, where readers could see every conversation they could not quite hear. It was full every day, and there was a queue for it by mid-morning. The demand for quiet had not disappeared. It had simply been given less space than it needed.

[3] This matters because quiet is not a luxury for a few serious readers. For a student sharing one small room with three brothers and sisters, or for an adult studying for an exam after a long shift at work, the library may be the only calm place available. These are often the very people whom the open, social library hopes to serve. A building can welcome them through the front door and still fail them once they are inside.

[4] I also worry about the books. When shelves are pushed to the walls to make room for flexible furniture, collections tend to shrink, and what remains is harder to browse. Yet browsing—finding a book you did not know you wanted—is one of the things a library does better than any search engine.

[5] None of this requires a return to the old treasury. It requires architects to treat quiet and collections as central needs and to give them as much careful thought as they give to cafés and workshops. A good library can be both a meeting place and a place to think, but only if it is designed to be both.

anchoring has little lasting effect on seagrass meadows.

show that dugongs are the main cause of seagrass loss.
provide scientific data about the number of dugongs.
use a familiar, appealing animal to draw attention to the overlooked meadow it depends on.

In many other bays, the meadows that store the most carbon shelter very few young fish.
Dugongs often travel between neighbouring bays.
Replanted seagrass shoots grow slowly in the first few years.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for **every** question, including the ones you got right, and check the reason given for each choice: make sure you chose the answer for the right reason.

List your wrong answers by category (Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, Integration of Knowledge and Ideas) and by trap: too extreme, too narrow, reversed, mixed-up details, or true but not in the passage.

Weak on main ideas, details and inferences? Go back to **Main Idea and Summary Questions**, **Detail Questions: "According to the Passage"**, **Relationships: Sequence, Cause–Effect and Comparison** and **Inference Questions: "It Can Reasonably Be Inferred"**.
Weak on word meaning, purpose and tone? Review **Words and Phrases in Context**, **Purpose, Function and Text Structure** and **Point of View, Tone and Perspective**.
Weak on the paired passages and evidence questions? Review **Paired Passages: Comparing Two Authors** and **Evaluating Arguments: Claims, Evidence and Reasoning**.
If you ran out of time, re-read **ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart** and practise one passage a day with a 10-minute timer.
